title: The bodhisattva ideal
hook: the Mahayana honors the bodhisattva who vows to help all; the two ideals are both honored in their own homes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the arahant: Patacara, freed after grief, who turned around and taught. Your line was fully freed. What did you set down, and what did your hands do instead? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

Long before he was the Buddha, the Pali Jataka tales say, he was a hare, a monkey king, a prince who gave away everything he had. Life after life, the stories follow one being on the long road to awakening. The Pali word for him in those lives is bodhisatta: the Buddha-to-be. The Theravada keeps those stories and still tells them, in temples and at festivals. Then the Mahayana sutras take that word and open the door wide. Not just one Buddha-to-be. Anyone can take the vow and walk that road, for the sake of every living being. Today, the bodhisattva.
screen: `A HARE, A MONKEY KING, A PRINCE.` → `THE BUDDHA-TO-BE.` → `THE DOOR OPENS WIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. In the Mahayana, a bodhisattva is someone who sets their heart on full awakening, not for themselves alone but in order to free all beings. That turning of the heart is called bodhicitta, the mind of awakening. Zen students chant a set of great vows, and the first is to free beings without number. Second, the long patience. The Indian poet-monk Shantideva wrote a line that Tibetan teachers often quote: as long as space remains, and as long as beings remain, may I too remain, to ease the sorrows of the world. Some bodhisattvas have temples and festivals of their own: Avalokiteshvara, called Guanyin in China and Kannon in Japan, who hears the cries of the world. Kshitigarbha, who, tradition says, vowed not to rest until the hells are empty. Third, the two ideals in their own homes. The Theravada centers the arahant and honors the bodhisatta path of the Buddha himself. The Mahayana centers the bodhisattva and honors the arahants in its temple halls. Each home explains its own ideal in its own words, and neither needs the other to be smaller. Fourth, the week behind us. We closed the movements, then began walking the schools side by side. What all share: the truths, the jewels, ethics and practice. Then the three turnings and the different maps. Then the arahant, fully freed. Now the bodhisattva. Two ideals, both honored.
screen: `THE VOW TO FREE ALL BEINGS.` · `AS LONG AS SPACE REMAINS.` · `TWO IDEALS IN THEIR OWN HOMES.` · `THE WEEK: SHARED GROUND, TWO IDEALS.` · then, large: `BOTH HONORED.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to hold the two, if you'd like. Sit, and let the breath settle. On the in-breath, bring to mind Patacara, freed, turning back to teach. On the out-breath, bring to mind Guanyin, listening for the cries of the world. Don't weigh them against each other. Let each one be honored as its own home honors it. If one of them moves you more today, that's fine; just keep a little room for the other. The bell holds the time.
The bodhisattva ideal. One who sets their heart on awakening for the sake of all beings: the Buddha-to-be in the Jatakas, the open vow in the Mahayana. Today's word.
Your line: both honored. Today, when you hear two people describe a good life in different ways, try to name what is admirable in each before you choose. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists often take bodhisattva vows and recite them in temples and retreats, and honor bodhisattvas like Guanyin with chanting and offerings; Theravada Buddhists tell the Jataka stories of the Buddha's past lives as a bodhisatta.

fork.setup: a friend from a Theravada temple and a friend from a Zen temple each describe their ideal over dinner. what do you do?
options: let each explain their own, and honor both.
say they're the same thing and change the subject.
fork.reveal: both homes honor the other's figures in their own way: Theravada keeps the bodhisatta stories; Mahayana keeps the luohan halls.

original.note: Sanskrit bodhisattva (Pali bodhisatta): one set on awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bodhisattva is a kind of angel.
what it means: one who sets their heart on awakening in order to free all beings.
what a scholar hears: bodhisatta in the Pali Jatakas, the Buddha-to-be; the Mahayana sutras open the same path to anyone who takes the vow.

notes: Shantideva 10.55 is paraphrased (no quotation marks); confirm the paraphrase is faithful, and the claim 'many Tibetan teachers still recite' it (softer: 'Tibetan teachers often recite').
Kshitigarbha's vow not to rest until the hells are empty is given as 'tradition says'; confirm.
'Zen students chant a set of great vows, and the first is to free beings without number' — the count of vows is left out; confirm the paraphrase.
Jataka figures (hare, monkey king, generous prince Vessantara) given as examples; confirm the Theravada telling of Jatakas at festivals is a fair general description.
Week-end look-back covers days 1359–1365 (Movements closed; the truths; the jewels; ethics and practice; three turnings; arahant; bodhisattva).
Trapdoor avoids the etymology of bodhisattva by design (claims rule).

Editor: Shantideva line softened from 'still recited in Tibetan teaching' to 'Tibetan teachers often quote'; myth item 'the Mahayana honors arahants too' (a near-repeat of day 1364's luohan myth) replaced with a Shantideva item.
